Wiener covering lemma

Words: 133 Articles: 1
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A finite collection of Euclidean open balls has a disjoint subcollection whose concentric triples cover the original union. Greedily retain a largest remaining ball and discard all intersecting ones. Each discarded ball has radius no greater than the retained one and lies in its triple. Lebesgue measure consequently bounds the original union by 3d times the sum of the retained volumes. This covering lemma is distinct from inverse-closedness results for the Wiener algebra.

Disjoint ball decomposition modulo null sets

Words: 63
Wiener covering lemma OurBigBook.com
Every open set of finite Lebesgue measure in Euclidean space is covered, up to a null set, by countably many pairwise disjoint open balls contained in it. At each stage cover a compact subset of the open remainder, choose a packing with the Wiener covering lemma, and remove its closed balls. A fixed positive fraction of the remaining measure is removed each time, while sphere boundaries are null.

Geometric measure theory

Measure theory OurBigBook.com

Vector measure (μ=(μ1​,…,μn​))

Words: 95 Articles: 2
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A finite-dimensional vector measure has scalar measures as components and a total variation norm of a measure defined using their joint vector norm. Finite variation controls every pairing with a bounded continuous vector test. Derivatives in the bounded-variation space are examples.

Vector Radon measure (M(Ω;Rn))

Words: 66 Articles: 1
Vector measure OurBigBook.com
A vector Radon measure has Radon measures as components. The vector form of the Riesz-Markov-Kakutani representation theorem identifies finite such measures with bounded functionals on C0​(Ω;Rn).

Polar decomposition of a vector measure (μ=σ∣μ∣,∣σ∣=1∣μ∣-a.e.)

Words: 46
Vector Radon measure OurBigBook.com
Each component of a finite vector measure is absolutely continuous with respect to its variation measure. The Radon-Nikodym theorem gives a vector density σ. Taking the variation measure of this representation gives ∣μ∣=∣σ∣∣μ∣, hence the unit-length property. For a BV derivative this separates the magnitude of variation from its local direction.

Standard Borel probability space ((X,B,μ))

Words: 45
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A probability space whose measurable space is isomorphic to a Borel subset of a complete separable metric space with its Borel sigma-algebra. This supplies a countable generating algebra and permits the disintegration theorem for a probability measure. Completions can be handled modulo null sets; conditional kernels are chosen on the underlying Borel model.

Measurable space ((Ω,F))

Words: 52 Articles: 1
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A measurable space is a set equipped with a sigma-algebra of measurable subsets. A measure space additionally specifies a measure on that sigma-algebra.

Standard Borel space

Words: 33
Measurable space OurBigBook.com
A standard Borel space is a measurable space isomorphic to a Borel set of a Polish space, with its Borel sigma-algebra. This measurable regularity permits the usual constructions of random samples and random counting measures, without requiring a particular compatible topology.

Hausdorff measure (Hs)

Words: 280 Articles: 4
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
Hausdorff measure measures a set by the small-scale cost of covers, using the sth powers of their diameters and a standard normalization. In Euclidean dimension one, H1 agrees with arc length on smooth curves; in particular a line segment has its usual length.

Scale-restricted Hausdorff content (Hδs​(F))

Words: 47
Hausdorff measure OurBigBook.com
For δ>0, the scale-restricted Hausdorff content is the infimum of ∑j​(diamUj​)s over countable covers of F by sets of diameter at most δ. It increases as δ decreases; its limit is the Hausdorff measure in the corresponding normalization. It is distinct from unrestricted Hausdorff content, which imposes no diameter bound.

Hausdorff dimension (dimH​E)

Words: 190 Articles: 2
Hausdorff measure OurBigBook.com
The Hausdorff dimension of a metric set E is dimH​E=inf{s≥0:Hs(E)=0}=sup{s≥0:Hs(E)=∞}, with the usual endpoint convention. Here Hs is Hausdorff measure, obtained from covers by sets of small diameter with cost equal to the sum of their diameters to the power s. It measures small-scale geometric size and can be nonintegral. A probability measure with μ(B(x,r))≤Crs supplies a lower bound dimH​E≥s: every cover must have total s-cost at least 1/C, up to a fixed diameter convention.

Pressure upper bound for Hausdorff dimension (P(γ∗​)=0 ⟹ dimH​F≤γ∗​)

Words: 62
Hausdorff dimension OurBigBook.com
Suppose shrinking interval covers of F have length-power sums with logarithmic growth rate P(γ), and P is strictly decreasing with zero γ∗​. For every γ>γ∗​ those sums tend to zero exponentially. The definition of Hausdorff measure then gives Hγ(F)=0, hence the displayed upper bound. A matching lower bound requires additional information and does not follow from this covering argument alone.

Hausdorff dimension of a connected set

Words: 44
Hausdorff dimension OurBigBook.com
A connected subset C of Euclidean space containing distinct points a,b has Hausdorff dimension at least one. The Lipschitz map x↦∣x−a∣ maps C onto a set containing [0,∣b−a∣], since continuous images of connected spaces are connected. A Lipschitz map cannot increase Hausdorff dimension, whereas an interval has Hausdorff dimension one. Consequently any set of Hausdorff dimension less than one is totally disconnected.

Null set (μ(N)=0)

Words: 63 Articles: 1
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A measurable set N is a null set for a measure μ when μ(N)=0. A property holds almost everywhere when its exceptions lie in a null set. With a complete measure, every subset of a null set is measurable and is itself a null set.

Borel null set

Words: 24
Null set OurBigBook.com
A Borel set of Lebesgue measure zero. Every Lebesgue-null set is contained in a Borel null set, by outer regularity; consequently testing all Borel null sets suffices in the definition of a Sierpiński set.

Random measure

Words: 27
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A random measure assigns a measure μω​ to each outcome so that ω↦μω​(A) is a random variable for every measurable A. A finite-variation process gives pathwise signed random measures through Lebesgue–Stieltjes integration.

Measurable partition (ξ)

Words: 252 Articles: 6
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A countable measurable partition is a countable family of pairwise disjoint measurable sets whose union has full measure. Its members are its atoms; null atoms can be discarded in statements made almost everywhere.

Partition atom (A∈ξ)

Words: 57
Measurable partition OurBigBook.com
A partition atom is a member of a measurable partition. For a finite or countable partition, each cell is an atom of a sigma-algebra generated by that partition, whose measurable sets are unions of cells. A partition atom need not be an atom of a measure: an interval cell with positive Lebesgue measure can be split into smaller positive-measure sets that lie outside the generated partition sigma-algebra.

Entropy of a countable measurable partition (Hμ​(ξ))

Words: 138 Articles: 3
Measurable partition OurBigBook.com
For a countable measurable partition, its entropy is Hμ​(ξ)=−∑A∈ξ​μ(A)logμ(A), with 0log0=0. This extends entropy of a finite measurable partition and is allowed to be infinite.

Conditional information function (Iμ​(ξ∣G))

Words: 118 Articles: 2
Entropy of a countable measurable partition OurBigBook.com
For a measurable partition ξ and a sigma-algebra G, the conditional information function is
Iμ​(ξ∣G)=−∑A∈ξ​1A​logEμ​[1A​∣G].
(1)
The conditional expectation in this formula is positive almost everywhere on A. Without conditioning, the information is Iμ​(ξ)(x)=−logμ(ξ(x)).
Maximal inequality for conditional information functions
Words: 53
Conditional information function OurBigBook.com
For increasing sigma-algebras Gn​, put fn​=Iμ​(ξ∣Gn​) and F=supn​fn​. For each atom A∈ξ and t≥0,
μ(A∩{F>t})≤e−t.
(2)
Together with the bound by μ(A) and the tail integral formula for moments, this yields ∫Fdμ≤Hμ​(ξ)+1. The inequality follows by stopping the conditional-expectation martingale E[1A​∣Gn​] the first time it falls below e−t.
Conditional entropy of a countable measurable partition (Hμ​(ξ∣G))
Words: 31
Conditional information function OurBigBook.com
The conditional entropy is the integral of the conditional information function. Its chain rule expresses the entropy of a join of measurable partitions as unconditional entropy plus conditional entropy. Conditioning reduces entropy, also for countable partitions of finite entropy.

Join of measurable partitions (ξ∨η)

Words: 25
Measurable partition OurBigBook.com
The join is the common refinement of two measurable partitions, with atoms given by their nonempty intersections. For a measure-preserving transformation, the block partition is ξ0n−1​=⋁j=0n−1​T−jξ.

Field of sets

Words: 28
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A Boolean algebra of subsets contains the empty set and is closed under finite unions and complements. It is consequently closed under finite intersections, differences, and symmetric differences.

Semiring of sets

Words: 38
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A semiring of sets contains the empty set, is closed under intersections, and has the property that the difference of two members is a finite disjoint union of members. Predictable rectangles form a semiring generating the predictable sigma-algebra.

Monotone class

Words: 97 Articles: 2
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A monotone class of sets is closed under increasing countable unions and decreasing countable intersections.

Monotone class theorem

Words: 82 Articles: 1
Monotone class OurBigBook.com
The monotone class theorem says that the smallest monotone class containing an algebra of sets equals the sigma-algebra generated by that algebra. It extends identities proved on a generating algebra to the full sigma-algebra.

Functional monotone-class theorem

Words: 48
Monotone class theorem OurBigBook.com
A vector space of bounded functions containing constants and indicators of a generating pi-system, and closed under uniformly bounded monotone pointwise limits, contains all bounded functions measurable for the generated sigma-algebra. This function version extends identities established on elementary integrands to every bounded measurable integrand.

Measurable function

Words: 154 Articles: 4
Measure theory OurBigBook.com
A function f:(X,A)→(Y,B) between measurable spaces is measurable when f−1(B)∈A for every B∈B.

Essential range (essranμ​m)

Words: 44
Measurable function OurBigBook.com
The essential range of a measurable function m is the set of scalars z for which μ({x:∣m(x)−z∣<ε})>0 for every ε>0. It depends on the measure as well as the function. On a nonzero L2 space over a sigma-finite measure, it describes the spectrum of a real multiplication operator when m is real.

Measurability (f−1(E)∈A)

Words: 46
Measurable function OurBigBook.com
Measurability is the property that inverse images of measurable target sets are measurable in the source space. For a stochastic process, joint measurability in time and sample is a different condition from the separate adaptedness condition at each fixed time. The predictable sigma-algebra and progressive measurability encode particular joint measurability requirements.

Borel measurable function

Words: 28
Measurable function OurBigBook.com
A function into a topological space is Borel measurable when the inverse image of every Borel set is measurable. Equivalently, it is measurable when the target carries its Borel sigma-algebra.

Composition of measurable functions

Words: 18
Measurable function OurBigBook.com
If f:(X,A)→(Y,B) and g:(Y,B)→(Z,C) are measurable, then g∘f is measurable because
(g∘f)−1(C)=f−1(g−1(C)).

Thus Y>c implies X≥c, Y<c implies X≤c, and Y=c implies X=c, outside a null set. Using a countable family of rational c separates any unequal real values and proves the claim. Since bn​(U)→U, the generated limiting sigma-algebra contains U up to null sets. For every event A in any finite-stage sigma-algebra, convergence in the L1 norm gives E[Y1A​]=E[f(U)1A​]. Cutting and stacking constructs measure-preserving transformations from towers of equal-measure levels. Cut a tower into equal-width subcolumns, add new spacer levels, and stack the resulting columns. Map each level to the one above by a measure-preserving identification; subsequent stages extend the partial map. When uncovered and top-level measures tend to zero, the limiting map is defined modulo null sets.

Cut the current tower into three equal subcolumns, place one spacer above the middle, and stack left to right. With initial width 2/3 and height one on a unit interval, level counts and widths are hj​=(3j+1−1)/2 and wj​=2/3j+1. Tower measure tends to one, using total spacer measure 1/3. A continuous self-map of a compact metric space is uniquely ergodic when it has exactly one invariant Borel probability measure. An irrational rotation of the circle is uniquely ergodic: invariance multiplies its nonzero-index Fourier coefficients by nontrivial phases, forcing those coefficients to vanish. The Stone-Weierstrass theorem then identifies the invariant measure as normalized Lebesgue measure.

Ergodicity OurBigBook.com
A probability measure-preserving transformation T is weakly mixing when, for every pair of measurable sets A,B, the average absolute correlation discrepancy tends to zero:
N1​∑n=0N−1​∣μ(T−nA∩B)−μ(A)μ(B)∣⟶0.
(24)
Equivalently, the correlations converge to their products in convergence in density of a sequence, its Cartesian product with itself is an ergodic transformation, or its product with every ergodic transformation is ergodic. The absolute values are essential: signed Cesaro convergence of a sequence of the correlations to their products characterizes ergodic transformations and does not imply weak mixing. For example, the transformation interchanging two equally weighted points has discrepancy (−1)n/4 for a singleton A=B: its signed average tends to zero while its average absolute discrepancy stays 1/4.

Tail measurability and block conditional entropy given the infinite future give H(β∣γ)≥(n+r)h. Thus H(γ)≤H(β)−(n+r)h+nε. Divide by n, then let n→∞ and ε↓0, proving hμ​(T,α)=0. A measure is inner regular on its measurable sets if their measures are suprema of the measures of contained compact sets. Equivalently it assigns finitely additive values in I to clopen sets. Locally constant functions are uniformly dense, so integration extends uniquely from finite sums. Countable additivity in the usual real-measure sense is not imposed. The coefficient ring may have infinite residue field and need not be compact.

Let I be a complete discrete valuation ring with a continuous Zp​-algebra structure. Every continuous function on Zp​ with values in I has a unique uniformly convergent expansion in the binomial polynomials, with an​=Δnf(0). This is the coefficient-ring version of the Mahler theorem. To see that an​→0, approximate the function modulo any power of the maximal ideal by a function of period pk. In the expansion of (E−1)pk, all intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by p, while (Epk−1) kills the periodic function. Iterating makes its differences vanish modulo the prescribed ideal power. Finite differences do not increase the uniform norm, so the same conclusion holds for the original function. Binomial inversion gives agreement at the nonnegative integers, and their density in the p-adic integers gives the expansion everywhere. This gives the dual description of p-adic measures by arbitrary bounded sequences of binomial moments, and hence the Amice transform.

Every finite positive Borel measure on Euclidean space is inner regular by compact sets and outer regular by open sets. For an open set U, the compact sets {x:∣x∣≤n, dist(x,Uc)≥1/n} increase to U, so continuity from below of a measure gives inner approximation. The empty complement is handled by compact balls. The class of Borel sets admitting both approximations is closed under complements: interchange inner and outer approximations, then truncate the inner closed set by a large compact ball, using finiteness of the measure. For a countable union, approximate its components from outside with summable errors, and approximate finitely many components from inside after making the remaining union's measure small. Thus this class is a sigma-algebra containing the open sets. In particular, a finite measure carried by a Borel null set has compact subsets of that carrier capturing arbitrarily nearly all its mass.

Composition of covers gives (f:u)≤(f:h)(h:u), so Iu​(f) is uniformly bounded while Iu​(h)=1. It is invariant under left translation, homogeneous, monotone and subadditive. As the support of u shrinks to the identity, its additivity defect tends to zero: use the continuous proportions fi​/(f1​+f2​+δp), with a cutoff p positive on both supports, whose oscillations are small on every translate of that small support. For finitely many translations, apply the Schauder-Tychonoff fixed-point theorem to the average of their induced affine dual maps. A fixed functional is stationary under this average. For each real continuous f, its orbit function h(g)=ϕ(lg​f) is continuous on the compact subgroup generated by those translations and satisfies a finite averaging identity. At a maximum, every summand must attain that same maximum; iteration and density of the positive-word semigroup force h to be constant. Thus the functional is fixed by each of the finitely many translations. Compactness and the finite intersection property now give a functional invariant under every translation. This controls the measure of subsequent batches without assuming that a prescribed null subset is itself a countable union of compact null sets.

The essential infimum and essential supremum are the two almost-everywhere order bounds; this section defines the upper bound.
The essential supremum of a measurable function is the least number M such that f≤M almost everywhere. It equals the L∞ norm for a nonnegative function and, on a finite measure space, ∥f∥p​→∥f∥∞​ as p→∞.
